method: Second process-chemistry pass: smoke taint, juice solids/turbidity, Brett risk window and sulfur-dioxide effectiveness. Published risk thresholds remain source-backed records; game transforms remain derived.

facts: Excessive inorganic nitrogen can increase ethyl-acetate/ester-taint risk.
Higher initial YAN or DAP additions can leave residual YAN in finished wine, which can provide nutrient for spoilage organisms under some conditions.
YAN influences fermentation rate and heat production as well as fermentation bouquet.
White-juice solids level affects fermentation kinetics, aroma profile and reductive/oxidative risk.
In an AWRI study across three white varieties, 100 NTU was described as the best compromise among tested 15–350 NTU treatments for fruit aroma versus sluggish/reductive risk.
Very high solids can increase susceptibility to oxidation because grape-skin polyphenol oxidase is concentrated in solids.
AWRI identifies the period after primary fermentation and through/after malolactic fermentation before effective sulfur-dioxide addition as a critical Brettanomyces risk window.
Slow MLF and prolonged unsulfured storage increase risk.
Excess residual nitrogen can contribute to spoilage-organism growth under some circumstances.
The antimicrobial and antioxidant effectiveness of sulfur dioxide depends strongly on wine pH because the molecular fraction decreases as pH rises.
Higher-pH wine therefore requires more free SO2 to achieve the same molecular SO2 level.
Repeated small additions can yield a lower useful free-SO2 fraction than an appropriately sized addition because more SO2 can become bound.
Smoke-derived volatile phenols can be absorbed by grapes and glycosylated into non-volatile precursors.
Phenolic glycosides can release volatile phenols during fermentation, barrel or bottle ageing, and in-mouth, so apparent smoke character can change with time.
Smoke-taint risk depends on vine growth stage, grape variety, smoke composition and exposure duration and cannot be represented by smoke presence alone.
AWRI smoke analysis uses free volatile phenols plus glycosides rather than a single marker.
Key markers include guaiacol, cresols and glycosides such as guaiacol rutinoside, cresol rutinoside and syringol gentiobioside.
AWRI published cultivar-specific moderate/high grape marker levels associated with perceptible smoke risk in young/aged wines; thresholds are analytical risk guides, not universal sensory cutoffs.

Smoke-impact mitigation can include hand harvesting, excluding leaves, cooling fruit, separating press fractions, activated carbon, reverse osmosis or other treatments.
Remediation can alter wine composition/style and therefore must be modeled as a winemaking decision with tradeoffs rather than a free removal of smoke risk.
